answer:
Focus on self-serve for the next quarter. You have 30 paying customers, fast integration and evidence of repeatable demand. Enterprise has potential, but its requirements would consume your entire development capacity before procurement delivers dependable revenue.

Self-serve currently generates $6,300 monthly. Each logistics contract adds $7,500 in monthly recurring revenue once signed and live; even two would not cover your current burn. SOC 2, on-premises deployment and customization also introduce ongoing support costs for a three-person team.

If $45,000 is **net monthly cash burn**, you have approximately **14.2 months of runway**. Six to seven months of procurement would consume $270,000–$315,000, leaving roughly seven to eight months at unchanged burn. If $45,000 instead means expenses before revenue, current runway is about 16.5 months. Neither calculation includes additional enterprise costs. Annual upfront payment helps cash only when collected.

Keep usage-based pricing, but test a monthly minimum with included usage for new customers, plus higher-priced tiers for greater volume and capabilities. Preserve an easy entry point. Determine prices from customer value, processing costs and willingness to pay; the $210 average alone does not establish underpricing. Require commitments in exchange for volume discounts.

Prioritize improvements that remove observed activation and retention barriers. Over 90 days, track paying conversions, cohort retention, gross margin and expansion. Sustained 15% monthly growth would bring revenue near $9,600 by then, but four months is insufficient to assume it persists.

Reconsider enterprise if customers provide binding commitments, upfront funding sufficient to cover delivery, and requirements reusable across customers. Otherwise, speculative enterprise work spends scarce runway before validating a repeatable business.
